newsitem.title: INDIA: IATA outlines new safety measures after Guam crash.
newsitem.headline: IATA outlines new safety measures after Guam crash.

text.p: The International Air Transport Association (IATA) said on Tuesday it is promoting measures it hopes will cut airline accident rates by 50 percent over the next decade.

"I am never happy with air safety. It can always be improved. We are working towards decreasing the rate of accidents by half over the next eight to 10 years," IATA's director-general Pierre Jeanniot told a news conference.
He said air traffic would double in the next eight to 10 years. He also said the cost of air traffic control had doubled to 10 percent per landing from five percent five years ago.
"After the Guam crash, IATA has started recommending ground proximity warning devices to its member airlines. These devices will warn pilots when they try and land a little too soon," he said.
A Korean Airlines Boeing 747 crashed before landing on the Pacific island of Guam last Wednesday, killing 227 of the 254 people on board.

The aircraft crashed in jungle on its approach to the island's airport. The same day, Guam airport's glidescope indicator, a key navigational device that guides an aircraft in for a landing, was shut for maintenance.
Without the glidescope, pilots have to use radar beacons for an instrument landing.
Jeanniot said IATA was working towards worldwide satellite coverage for aircraft navigation in 15 years. He said satellites can monitor the position of aircraft to within a few meters.

"This system is already available on the Australia, New Zealand and Fiji sector, and will soon cover the Singapore-Delhi air corridor. We are also pressing India to implement it for the Delhi-Bombay sector."
There are more than 20 flights a day between Delhi and Bombay, operated by two state carriers Indian Airlines and Air India as well as several private airlines.
Jeanniot said IATA's endeavour was to implement the satellite navigation system over China, Iran and Afghanistan soon to cover the complete air corridor from Asia to Europe.
He said air traffic control resources were strained in countries like India with the growth in air traffic. IATA was urging governments to modernise air traffic control as soon as possible, he said.
The worst mid-air collision in aviation history occurred last November near Delhi when a Saudi Arabian airliner and a Kazakh transport plane collided killing 349 people.

A report by India's aviation regulator, the Directorate-General of Civil Aviation, cited 39 cases of air safety violations, including an unspecified number of near-collisions, between August 1994 and July 1996 in Indian skies.
